newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS--U.S. dependence on LATAM oil grows.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS--U.S. dependence on LATAM oil grows.

text.p: The growing U.S. dependence on foreign oil continues to shift away from the volatile Middle East and toward the relatively safer producers in the Americas, according to latest Department of Energy figures.
But some experts warn that there may be too much complacency over security of supply.

Indeed, on the eve of leaving office last week, outgoing Energy Secretary Hazel R. O'Leary warned that with crude oil imports up above 50 percent of needs the U.S. remains at the mercy of producers, no matter their location.

"We need a wake-up call," said Energy Secretary Hazel R. O'Leary in an interview in The New York Times last Sunday. "Almost any short-term dislocation, from a place like Venezuela, which is in fact our largest source...would get our attention in the short-term."

According to latest DOE figures, released Thursday, MidEast crude oil imports in the first 11 months of 1996 accounted for about 20 percent of total U.S. gross crude oil imports, down from 20.5 percent for all of 1995 and compared to about 31 percent in 1990.

The slack has been taken up largely by Latin America, which has increased its imports to the U.S. by more than 50 percent since the Gulf War in 1990 to more than 2.9 million barrels a day last year, with Venezuela alone accounting for 1.3 million bpd, the DOE data show.
The LATAM region represents about 39 pct of total gross crude oil imports of 7.5 million bpd into the U.S. between January and November 1996, compared to 36 pct for all of 1995, and 25 pct for 1990.
DOE's monthly report also showed the U.S. imports about 52 percent of its crude oil and products supply in the Jan-Nov 1996 period, compared to 41 pct in 1995 and 35 pct in 1990.

"Venezuela is...the largest exporter to the U.S. and people are less concerned about the political situation in Venezuela than in the Middle East," said Dimitris Tsitsiragos, investment officer at the International Finance Corporation, the private sector affiliate of the World Bank.
But he and others warn that though the geopolitic risk may have lessened, foreign oil dependence has risen above 50 percent and the U.S. remains vulnerable to price shocks.
"We are still affected when there is turmoil anywhere," said John Lastelic of the American Petroleum Institute, a Washington-based trade association.
"But we cannot produce more oil because of government policies that restrict drilling," Lastelic adds.
Oil industry players say reduced taxes and restrictions on drilling, particularly in the controversial Alaskan National Wildlife Refuge, is the only way to turn the situation around.
Short of that, said Paulo S. Nery, a senior consultant at Pace Consultants Inc, the U.S. in 2000 will be importing 70 to 80 percent of its projected demand of 18.7 million bpd.
"(U.S.) crude oil production has been dropping two percent for the past 15 years across the U.S. and the only way to change that is to allow companies to explore for oil," said Nery.
But environmentalists, which have lobbied the government hard to protect against more drilling in the U.S., say they won't budge on Alaska and that other energy resources can be pursued.

Until that happens, Pace's Nery estimates that Venezuela, which plans to double its production to about 6.1 million bpd and expand refinery ownership in the U.S., will continue to be the largest U.S. supplier, forecast by Pace at 1.6 million bpd in 2000.
Mexico, Colombia, Argentina and Canada, which are also eyeing increased production rates, will follow as among important suppliers to meet U.S. demand.
